clean_text: Why is electricity in Malaysia getting more expensive, and why does building clean energy feel so slow and disjointed? Right now, when we build massive solar farms, we hand the whole job to private developers. It sounds fine on paper, but in reality, it is a messy, expensive headache. A private company has to spend two years hunting for land, arguing with state land offices, begging the banks for high-interest commercial loans, and paying heavy legal fees before they even put a single screw in the ground. By the time they actually build the farm, they need to charge high rates on their electricity just to pay back their expensive loans and make a big profit for their shareholders. On top of that, because they only build small farms one at a time, they buy panels and batteries at regular retail prices from overseas. When construction finishes, the contractors pack up and leave. We learn very little, we build almost nothing locally, and you end up paying for all those unnecessary middleman costs on your monthly electric bill. This is where Energie comes in. Energie is the idea of having one dedicated, 100% state-owned national company whose sole job is to build utility-scale solar and battery storage at massive volume. Think of Energie not as a government office that does construction itself, but as the ultimate master planner and friction-killer. Here is why it works: ✓Cheap sovereign funding. ✓Private companies borrow money at 6% to 8% interest because banks treat them as risky. The government can back projects using sovereign sukuk at around 3.8% to 4%. When your borrowing cost is nearly cut in half and there are no private shareholders demanding giant annual dividends, the electricity produced is fundamentally cheaper from day one. ✓Clearing the path beforehand. Energie does not waste years hunting for private land. The state already owns thousands of hectares of idle mining land, reservoir water surfaces, and open buffer zones. Energie identifies the land, clears the approvals, and connects directly to the main power grid before touching a single solar panel. ✓Letting builders do what they do best. Instead of forcing contractors to become bankers and land negotiators, Energie simply tenders out the construction. It hands private contractors a shovel-ready site with guaranteed cash ready to go. Construction companies compete purely on who can build it best, fastest, and cheapest. ✓Insane bulk buying power. Instead of ordering a few panels for one small farm, Energie orders massive pipelines of equipment straight from the biggest factories in the world. Buying at gigawatt scale gets you direct factory-gate discounts that no private developer can ever touch. ✓Real skills and real industry for our generation. Because Energie guarantees decades of steady, continuous projects, local factories can finally afford to manufacture mounting structures, cables, high-voltage transformers, and battery systems right here at home. It means vocational schools and engineering universities can train young Malaysians on live, world-class clean energy systems, creating permanent, skilled technical careers instead of temporary gig jobs. Energie takes what the state is great at ; low-cost financing, land access, and long-term national planning and combines it with what the private sector is great at ie fast, competitive construction. The result is simple: cheaper power bills for regular households, real local industries, and a national energy grid built to last.

clean_text: Giving Credit Where Credit Is Due: Rafizi Ramli's Reform Agenda in Just 2½ Years Politics aside, any fair assessment of Rafizi Ramli's tenure as Minister of Economy should recognise the scale of reforms and initiatives introduced within a relatively short period of about 2½ years. Among the major initiatives associated with his ministry were: Inisiatif Pendapatan Rakyat (IPR) to help lower-income households generate sustainable income. Progressive Wage Policy (Gaji Progresif) aimed at raising wages through skills and productivity growth. Akademi in Industry (AiI) to strengthen workforce skills and industry readiness. Digital Leadership Programmes (EDL) to prepare talent for the digital economy. Innovathon and innovation-driven programmes to encourage entrepreneurship and technological development. ARM semiconductor ecosystem initiatives to move Malaysia higher up the global value chain. Renewable energy and green economy planning to position Malaysia for future industries. Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) to attract high-value investments and deepen regional economic integration. Implementation of the MADANI Economic Framework, which sought to provide a long-term economic direction beyond short-term political cycles. Whether one supports or opposes Rafizi politically, it is difficult to deny that his ministry pursued a broad agenda touching wages, technology, industrial policy, skills development, investment attraction, and economic restructuring. Why Some Supporters Are Impressed Malaysian argue that many Malaysian ministers spend years managing existing systems, whereas Rafizi attempted to introduce structural reforms addressing long-standing issues such as: Stagnant wage growth. Dependence on low-skilled labour. Limited industrial upgrading. Weak technology transfer. Skills mismatches in the workforce. Overreliance on traditional investment models. They see these initiatives as laying foundations that may take years to show their full results. The "What If" Question: Rafizi as Prime Minister Malaysian often ask: If Rafizi could push this many reforms as Minister of Economy, what could he achieve as Prime Minister? The argument is that, as Prime Minister, he would have greater authority to coordinate reforms across ministries, including: Labour market reform. Education reform. Industrial policy. Digital transformation. Public sector efficiency. Institutional reforms. Anti-corruption measures. Fiscal and subsidy restructuring. Advocates believe this could accelerate Malaysia's transition toward a high-income, innovation-driven economy. The Reality Of course, being Prime Minister is very different from being a minister. Success depends not only on ideas, but also on: Building political coalitions based on integrity and accountability. Managing Parliament with transparency and openness. Working with state governments on MP allocations to ensure fairness, supported by an MP Performance Portal to promote transparency and accountability. Navigating civil service implementation while monitoring progress through a Civil Service Performance Portal. Balancing economic, social, and ethnic considerations through a new National Security and People's Wellbeing Act (Akta Keselamatan dan Kesejahteraan Rakyat). Ultimately, voters will judge reforms not by announcements, but by outcomes: higher wages, better jobs, stronger local businesses, affordable living costs, and improved quality of life. Still, even critics would likely agree that introducing and pursuing such a wide range of economic initiatives within 2½ years represents one of the more ambitious reform efforts seen from a Malaysian Minister of Economy in recent years. clean_text: Malam Habu, I am interested in this discussion, as a student of energy economics & policy management. It is a topic that I believe should be debated. I actually support @atiku 's argument for the reintroduction of a fuel subsidy; but I do not mean the old, opaque subsidy regime, that is open to abise & corruption. That your "𝑮𝒐𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒏𝒐𝒓𝒔 𝒘𝒐𝒖𝒍𝒅 𝒂𝒈𝒓𝒆𝒆 𝒌𝒆𝒉", caught my attention because I have always argued that they, & the FG are the biggest beneficiaries of all these jumbos & not the common man. For me, Dr. Hidima, a targeted, capped, transparent subsidy that reduces the price of petrol to, for instance, ₦400–₦500 per litre for Nigerians, while the govt covers only the verified differential is POSSIBLE! As per your maths: A market price of say, ₦1,300 means the govt absorbs ₦900 per litre: 50 million litres per day × ₦900 = ₦45 billion per day This translates to: ₦1.35 trillion per month ₦16.4 trillion per year! At first glance, this appears unsustainable. However, this is where the discussion should be interesting. Taiwo Oyedele has noted that the government mobilised approximately ₦15.8 trillion for the Federation over 31 months following the subsidy removal and FX reforms. This averages about ₦510 billion per month. Thus, a ₦16 trillion annual subsidy would indeed be substantial. For me, no one should suggest that govt should issue an uncapped ₦16 trillion expenditure. The question, for me Malam Habu is, why can't we design a system that subsidises only the first 15–20 litres purchased by households weekly? This is doable. For Example, Malaysia monitors fuel consumption using 𝐌𝐲𝐊𝐚𝐝 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧, similar to our NIN and caps subsidized RON95 petrol at RM1.99 per litre up to a monthly limit (such as 200–300 litres). The same Malaysia does support its older citizens of say, 60 & above with 50% fare reductions on select public transit systems like Rapid KL and KTMB. Not only that, low-income older adults may qualify for specific welfare grants like Bantuan Warga Emas (BWE). Why can't we focus subsidies on public transportation and commercial operators rather than universal consumption? Why can't we gradually phase out the subsidy in line with improvements in domestic refining capacity? This was what a lot of us expected. For instance, as PH1 comes on stream, 35% subsidy would go. As PH2 comes on stream, another 35% goes. When Warri comes alive, another 20% goes, and when Kaduna comes onboard, 100% subsidy would be removed! Again, why can't we design a subsidy framework that renders smuggling economically unviable? 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐞. The technological tools already exist to monitor petroleum distribution. 𝐖𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐝! We can implement digital truck registration systems, depot-to-station tracking, electronic invoicing, GPS and geofencing technologies, and full reconciliation of refinery output, depot receipts, logistics movements, and retail sales. Our organisation can provide this service perfectly! Stations whose reported volumes are inconsistent with their customer base can be audited. Subsidy payments should be made strictly on the basis of verified domestic consumption. If a litre is diverted across the border illegally, it should not attract any subsidy payment. This is straightforward. Also, what I observe is that, anytime we are debating on this issue, it is always presented as a binary choice: Nigerians, you either buy fuel at ₦1,300 per litre OR we "waste" ₦16 trillion paying subsidy. 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐬𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐲. 𝐔𝐧𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐧’𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨, there is defined a third option: 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. Government can subsidise essential and vulnerable consumption without extending the same benefit to unlimited or luxury consumption, as explained above & it is done in other countries.

WEEKEND RANTING: MALAYSIA NATIONAL PASTIME - THE ENDLESS COMPLAINT ABOUT THE PRIME MINISTER 1. You know, back in the day, folks used to gather at kopitiams, sip their kopi O, and gripe about politics like it was a second job. Fast forward to today, and nothing’s changed, except now the complaints come faster, louder, and with more flair. And poor DS Anwar Ibrahim? He’s the lightning rod for it all. 2. One camp says he’s too establishment. “He’s been around forever, man. Reformasi? Please. He’s the system dressed up as change.” That’s the line. They don’t care that he’s survived decades of political trench warfare. To them, that’s proof he’s part of the machine. 3. Then you have got the economic purists. These guys treat every policy like a personal insult. Subsidy reforms? Too cruel. Inflation measures? Too slow. Cost of living? Still unbearable. If DS Anwar handed out free rice, they’d complain the grains weren’t polished enough. 4. It’s the same old tune: • If he compromises, he’s weak. • If he stands firm, he’s authoritarian. • If he listens, he’s indecisive. • If he ignores, he’s arrogant. 5. In Malaysia, the Prime Minister is expected to be a saint, a savior, and a pasar malam vendor all rolled into one. And even then, someone will say the satay sticks are too short. 6. From my bodo2 observations, the louder the noise, the clearer the proof that DS Anwar is actually moving the needle. Nobody wastes breath on irrelevance. The fact that he is catching fire from every direction means he is poking sacred cows, shaking comfort zones, and forcing Malaysians to face truths they’d rather sweep under the carpet. 7. So yes, the complaints will never stop. But maybe that’s the ultimate badge of honor in Malaysian politics: if everyone’s yelling, it means you’re alive. And in a country where invisibility is the easiest way to survive, being loudly criticized might just be the only sign you’re doing something real.
